metadata.title: How does PISA measure students’ ability to collaborate?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus brief describes the design of the PISA 2015 collaborative problem-solving assessment rather than reporting an analysis with an explicit analytic subsample. It states that students in 52 education systems completed the assessment, but it does not specify whether OECD/PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in any statistical estimation. For any downstream analysis using PISA microdata, analysts should use the official PISA student/sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the dataset to account for the complex two-stage sampling and clustering of students within schools. The brief does not report any weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate procedures, so weighting cannot be confirmed from the text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive assessment-design explainer (PISA in Focus) and does not report an empirical model that uses PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. Because no PV-based dependent variable is analyzed and no missing-data strategy for an estimation model is described, plausible-value handling and missing-data handling are not applicable/reported in the sense required for empirical ML/statistical extraction. The text focuses on how collaborative problem solving is operationalized via computer-based tasks and competencies rather than on estimation procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2015 collaborative problem-solving assessment administered to students in 52 education systems; the brief does not describe any further analytic filtering (e.g., grade restrictions, task completion thresholds, or exclusions).

data.outcome_summary: PISA 2015 introduced a new computer-administered assessment of collaborative problem solving, extending beyond the 2012 individual problem-solving framework. The assessment uses computer simulations in which students are placed in a team and must answer quiz-show-like questions about the fictional country of Xandar, with computer agents whose behavior can be controlled to standardize partner interactions. Competence is defined through four individual problem-solving processes plus three collaborative competencies, yielding 12 specific skills that are targeted by test items. The brief reports participation of around 125,000 students across 52 education systems, but it does not provide scoring benchmarks, model performance metrics, or an estimation strategy. It also summarizes evidence that computer-agent collaboration is a reasonable approximation of human-human collaboration, supporting the validity of the measurement approach.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical predictive/causal study paper; it is an OECD PISA in Focus explainer of the assessment construct and task design. As a result, there are no reported ML algorithms, no PV/missing-data handling for an estimation model, and no quantitative outcome metrics to extract into main_findings. Country-level sample sizes and specific weighting/replicate procedures are also not provided in the text, so those fields remain sparse by design.
